chunks: And what Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr al-Bazanti narrated from Abd al-Karim ibn Amr from Abi Basir from Abi Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:
The curse (l'an) does not take effect until the man has entered with his wife, and the curse does not occur except with the denial of the child.

These two hadiths do not contradict what we have previously mentioned from the reports that the curse takes effect by accusation (qadhf), because the apparent meaning of the Quran supports the first hadith. Allah the Exalted said: 'And those who accuse their wives and have no witnesses except themselves' [the verse].

And it did not stipulate in it the denial of the child, and since the first hadith, if the intended meaning was the denial of the curse from the accusation in all cases, it would be contradictory, because he said: 'The curse does not occur except with the denial of the child,' then he said: 'And when the man accuses his wife, he curses her.'
And if the intended meaning was what some people went to, it would be contradictory, as you see.
The resolution in these two reports is that the one who curses in the accusation is not a 'li'an' partner merely by speech, until he adds to the speech the claim of witnessing (mu'ayanah).
And his ruling is not so in the denial of the child, because whenever he denies the child, the curse becomes obligatory upon him, even if he does not claim the witnessing of the immorality.
Thus the two rulings differ in the denial of the child and mere accusation from this aspect.
And that which indicates that the claim of witnessing is a condition in the accusation is what he narrated:

key_terms.اللَّعْنُ: The ritual of mutual cursing between spouses in case of accusation of adultery.

ai.seo_question: What are the conditions for the ritual of L'an (mutual cursing) in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi resolves the apparent contradiction between hadiths by distinguishing between mere verbal accusation (qadhf), which requires a claim of eyewitnessing to trigger l'an, and denial of paternity, which obligates l'an regardless of claimed witness. This nuance aligns with the Quranic text in Surah An-Nur, which specifies the procedure for those who accuse their wives without witnesses, highlighting that the ritual's applicability depends on the specific nature of the claim. The scholar emphasizes that this distinction preserves the consistency of the legal rulings derived from the Quran and the Imams.
